This architecture shows how to route requests through a gateway, apply policies, and instrument every call.

Client sends request with intent, optional tools, and context hints. Gateway selects route based on intent and policy (see Context routing). Apply budgets and safety filters; reject or adjust if needed. Dispatch to provider with prompt pack and tool allowlist. Return response with trace_id, route_used, and usage.

Policies per route: tools, safety filters, budgets, providers. Prompt packs versioned and linted; include vibe cues and refusal guidance. Observability: traces and metrics across gateway, provider, and tools.
Pattern: AI Integration pattern Platform: Model Gateway Reference: MCP contract
Inputs: intent, context hints, allowed tools, prompt pack. Execution: uses MCP/gateway to call tools with schemas and allowlists. Outputs: response with citations, tool traces, and trace_id.
Use MCP for schemas and capability discovery. Enforce tool allowlists per route; block high-risk actions. Keep tool names and arguments consistent across providers.

Route agents through the gateway: budgets, safety filters, and provider selection. Keep prompt packs versioned; include refusal guidance and style cues. Fallback providers must share the same prompt pack and tool policy.
Log trace_id, route_used, tools invoked, and timing. Redact sensitive fields; ensure PII scrubbing is enabled. Run evaluation probes regularly for groundedness, safety, and latency.
Apply per-agent/client budgets for tokens and cost. Require refusals for disallowed topics; block banned tools by default. Use MCP schema validation to reject malformed requests.
Pattern: Model Context Protocol Pattern: AI Integration pattern Concept: Prompt engineering and vibe coding Task: Add a tool to MCP safely
Evaluation probes keep prompt and routing changes grounded.
Detect regressions early for prompts, routes, and tools. Make refusal and safety behaviors explicit. Compare providers and routes with the same test set.

Grounded answers: expect citations to specific docs. Safety/refusal: expect a safe refusal on disallowed topics. Latency: track time to first token and total response. Tool correctness: ensure tool calls match allowlists and arguments.

Use short, stable inputs; avoid ambiguous phrasing. Pair each probe with an expected output pattern (citations, refusal language, tool calls). Version probes with prompts and routes; run after every change.
Run against primary and fallback routes via the gateway. Capture trace_id, route_used, and tool logs. Store results next to prompts and configs for traceability.
Concept: Prompt engineering and vibe coding Pattern: AI Integration pattern Task: Run a prompt and vibe coding review

Model: capabilities differ (function calling, context length, safety). Track version and provider. Prompt pack: role, scope, style cues, refusal guidance, examples. Context: retrieved docs or tool outputs; must be selected and cited. Tools: schemas and allowlists via MCP/gateway. Safety and budgets: refusals, redaction, cost/latency caps.
Decide intent → pick route → apply prompt pack → attach context/tools → evaluate. Keep prompts, routes, and probes versioned together.
Use refusal guidance for safety; block high-risk tools by default. Enforce budgets per service and route. Require citations for grounded answers.

Fast iteration without cloud dependency. Lower cost for early exploration. Safer by default: no external data egress during prototyping.

Runtime: ollama or llama.cpp for chat and completion. Retrieval: SQLite + embeddings for small corpora; keep corpora under version control. Tools: MCP server with file/search utilities; logs stored locally.
Pin model versions; record hashes. Keep prompts and vibe cues in source control with linting. Store evaluation probes alongside data and regenerate scores after changes.

Make intent, tone, and constraints explicit. Keep prompts versioned and testable. Prevent drift while allowing controlled experimentation.

System framing: role, scope, and boundaries. Style cues: tone, concision, formatting, taboo words. Inputs: explicit slots for context and tools. Safety: instructions on refusal, citations, and redaction.
Use short, repeatable style cues instead of long prose. Keep a prompt changelog; pair changes with evaluation probes. Treat prompt packs as assets: versioned, linted, and reviewed.
Run evals against probes (grounded answers, safety refusals, latency). Compare outputs across providers via the Model Gateway. Capture drift in Prompt drift and promote fixes into patterns.
Pattern: AI Integration pattern Docs: Run a prompt/vibe coding review Templates: Prompt pack starter (to add)
Prompt routing keeps requests predictable across models, tools, and providers.

Map intents to prompt packs: one pack per task, with vibe cues and refusal guidance. Select routes based on capability and cost; keep fallbacks defined per family. Bind tool allowlists to prompts so models only call what you expect.

Define intent-to-route rules in the gateway; include required context fields. Pair each route with a prompt pack; store both under version control. Use MCP schemas to keep tool arguments strict and discoverable.
Run probes per intent: groundedness, safety refusal, and latency. Verify tool calls: ensure only allowed tools appear in logs. Compare outputs across providers to detect drift.
Pattern: AI Integration pattern Concept: Prompt engineering and vibe coding Task: Run a prompt and vibe coding review

PII scrubbing on by default; redact before logging. Tool allowlists per route; block high-risk actions unless explicitly approved. Budgets: tokens and cost per service, with alerts on soft thresholds. Authentication: short-lived tokens per client; separate write and read scopes.

Gateway: configure budgets and safety filters (see Model Gateway configuration). MCP: validate schemas; reject requests with missing required fields. Observability: emit trace_id, route_used, and tool metadata for every call.
Intentionally trigger blocked categories; expect safe refusal. Exceed soft budget to confirm alerting. Verify redaction in logs.

Documentation-first: concise, instructional, and reusable. No marketing tone; avoid long-form essays and personal narratives. State the page type and purpose quickly; keep sections scannable.
Clear, direct, and precise. Prefer active voice; keep sentences short. Use neutral language; avoid hype and speculation.
Lead with why/what; then how; then links to related docs. Use headings, bullets, and tables to keep content scannable. Keep intros short; move detail into ordered steps or references.
Every doc should include: title: <Title> description: <Short, specific description> tags: [tag1, tag2] last_reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD status: draft|stable topics: - <Use defined topics>
Link to related Platforms, Patterns, Docs, and Templates where relevant. Exploration entries must point to the systems/patterns/docs they reflect. Use Browse by topic for cross-navigation.
Keep snippets minimal; add language hints for copy buttons. Provide expected outputs when helpful; avoid long logs.
Add checklists for tasks; include verification and rollback where applicable.
Use headings in order (h2, h3…); avoid giant blocks of text. Keep tables simple; avoid excessive styling.

Use this reference when adding or reviewing MCP contracts.

{ "version": "0.2.0", "capabilities": { "tools": [ { "name": "fetch_customer_profile", "schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "customer_id": {"type": "string"}, "fields": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}} }, "required": ["customer_id"] } } ], "context": [ { "name": "docs-index", "schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": {"type": "string"}, "top_k": {"type": "integer", "default": 5} }, "required": ["query"] } } ] } }

Schema validation errors include the failing path and reason. Results include trace_id, tool name, and route or provider (if routed through a gateway). Errors are explicit: 401 auth failure, 403 blocked by policy, 429 rate limit, 500/503 tool/provider failures.
Apply per-tool auth and rate limits. Enforce allowlists for tools and context sources per route. Redact sensitive fields in logs; store only necessary outputs.

Use this checklist before deploying or auditing routes.

Route intent and families defined (chat, completion, embeddings). Providers listed with priority and fallbacks. Prompt pack version pinned; refusal and style cues present. Tool allowlist per route; schemas validated. Safety filters on; blocked categories defined. Budgets per service and route (tokens, cost); alerts configured. Logging: trace_id, route_used, tool names; PII redaction enabled.
Groundedness probe passes with citations. Safety/refusal probe blocks disallowed topics. Latency within target for primary and fallback. Tool call probe succeeds only for allowed tools.

Publish a new MCP tool with clear schema, safety controls, and observability.

Define the JSON schema and required fields. Keep names consistent with existing tools. Add the tool to the MCP server manifest and version it (e.g., v1.2.0). Enforce auth and rate limits for this tool in the server config. Update gateway policies to allow the tool only on specific routes. Deploy to staging and run sample calls with valid and invalid inputs.
Invalid inputs return schema errors, not silent failures. Logs include trace_id, route, and tool name. Tool is callable only on allowed routes.
Remove the tool from the manifest and redeploy. Tighten gateway policies to block the tool until issues are fixed.
Pattern: Model Context Protocol Docs: Safety and budgets for GenAI Platform: Model Gateway configuration
Confirm that routes enforce safety, tool allowlists, and budgets before production rollout.

Review route configs: tools, safety filters, blocked categories, budgets. Run negative tests: trigger blocked categories and expect safe refusals. Exceed soft budgets with test traffic; confirm alerts fire. Attempt disallowed tools; ensure the gateway rejects the call. Check logs for redaction and presence of trace_id and route_used.
Safety refusals occur with clear messages. Budget alerts fire and stop at hard limits. Disallowed tools are blocked; allowed tools succeed. Logs show redacted sensitive fields.
Tighten policies by disabling the route or removing tools. Lower budgets temporarily until issues are fixed.
Concept: Safety and budgets for GenAI Platform: Model Gateway configuration Pattern: AI Integration pattern
Get a local LLM + retrieval + MCP tool server running for experimentation.

Install ollama and pull a 7B model: ollama pull llama3. Start the runtime: ollama run llama3. Create a small docs corpus (e.g., ADRs) and embed into SQLite using text-embedding-3-small. Run an MCP server exposing search_docs and get_file tools over that corpus. Connect your agent/client to the MCP server and run a sample query.
Responses include trace_id and cite retrieved docs. Tool calls succeed and return expected content. Logs show no PII leakage.
Stop the runtime and MCP server; delete the local corpus DB if needed.

Ship AI features with a predictable workflow: design, evaluate, approve, ship, and monitor with rollback ready.

Shape the change Define user intent, guardrails, and success metrics. Identify routes, prompts, tools, and budgets that will change. Design with controls Add refusal rules, tool allowlists, budgets, redaction, and trace IDs. Document assumptions and rollback triggers in the change request. Evaluate before ship Run eval probes: happy-path, refusal, safety, regression. Capture metrics (success rate, refusal quality, latency, budget hit rate). Stage and gate Ship to staging with the same policies as prod. Require approval from an owner (product) and a safety/infra reviewer. Progressive rollout Start with low-traffic routes or a canary flag; enforce hard budgets. Watch traces/logs; block on incident noise or budget saturation. Operate and learn Track incidents with clear ownership. Capture observations in Exploration notes; feed fixes into docs and patterns.

Routes and tools documented; budgets and safety policies enforced. Evals passed for happy-path and refusal cases. Canary plan exists with rollback command or config toggle. Logging: redaction on, trace IDs present, errors searchable. Owners assigned for feature, safety, and on-call.
Disable the flag or route. Revert to last known good prompt/policy bundle. Pause tool allowlists if the issue is tool-related. Notify owners and log an incident entry.

Review a prompt (or pack) to ensure it meets style, safety, and evaluation requirements.

Collect the prompt, intended routes/models, and recent outputs. Check style cues: tone, concision, formatting, taboo words. Verify safety and refusal guidance; confirm tool allowlists. Ensure evaluation probes exist for groundedness, safety, and latency. Record changes and decisions in a prompt changelog.
Prompt includes explicit role, scope, style cues, and refusal guidance. Tool usage is explicit and matches gateway/MCP policies. Evaluation probes run cleanly across providers.
Revert to the previous prompt version in source control. Disable new prompt in gateway routes until fixes land.
Concept: Prompt engineering and vibe coding Exploration: Prompt drift Pattern: AI Integration pattern
Add a fallback provider for a route while keeping safety, budgets, and observability intact.

Update route config to include primary and fallback providers with clear priority. Keep prompt pack identical across providers; note any model-specific parameters. Ensure safety filters and tool allowlists are consistent for primary and fallback. Set budgets per provider if costs differ. Deploy to staging and run probes for groundedness, refusal, and latency across both providers.
route_used shows fallback when primary is down or fails checks. Safety and tool allowlists behave the same on fallback. Probes pass on both providers; latency within expected bounds.
Remove fallback entry and redeploy. Temporarily disable the route if both providers fail probes.
Pattern: AI Integration pattern Reference: LLM Routing Architecture Task: Audit gateway safety and budgets
Create a small, local retrieval setup to test prompts, routing, and grounding.

Prepare a corpus: export 20–50 docs (ADRs, runbooks) into a flat folder. Embed with a local script using text-embedding-3-small or a local embedding model; store vectors in SQLite. Expose a search_docs tool via MCP pointing to the SQLite index. Wire the tool into your client/agent and run sample queries with expected citations.
Search returns relevant docs with IDs and snippets. Tool calls log trace_id, query, and hit count. Responses include citations that map back to the corpus.
Stop the MCP server and delete the local index if needed.

Retention: default 7 days unless auditing requires longer. Dead-letter: required for regulated channels; point to audit-dlq. Encryption: enabled by default at rest and in transit.

Access to the platform management project. Node.js 20 or container runtime for CLI tasks. Network access to edge control plane endpoints.

Bootstrap the control plane Create a project with edgectl project create --name messaging-core. Verify access with edgectl auth status. Create core channels edgectl channel create --name user-events --retention 7d. edgectl channel create --name audit-log --retention 30d --dlq audit-dlq. Enable policies Apply defaults from policies/default.yaml and commit changes. Smoke test Publish a test event and confirm it is received by a sample consumer.
Control plane reachable. Baseline channels created and documented. CI secrets ready for usage steps.
Configure policies: Platform configuration. Apply routing patterns: Context routing pattern. Capture runbooks using the Runbook template.
Edge Messaging delivers low-latency event fanout at the edge for internal services. Readers can find procedures in the platform subpages and related patterns in the Context Routing pattern.
Managed messaging fabric that runs at edge locations. Targets service-to-service notifications, webhooks, and background triggers. Provides a narrow API to reduce operational surface area.
You need predictable fanout with single-digit millisecond delivery targets. You want a hosted option instead of running a queue per team. You plan to reuse governance patterns like Context Routing.

Channels: logical streams with retention and delivery policies. Producers: services publishing events via HTTPS or signed requests. Consumers: edge workers or services that subscribe with filters. Policies: declarative configs that set retention, retries, and dead-letter handling.

POST /tools name, schema, routes[], version timeout_ms, description Register before tools can be used. GET /routes n/a n/a Returns route definitions and policies. GET /health n/a n/a Includes provider connectivity details.

Field Description trace_id Correlates calls across Model Gateway and downstream logs. route_used The route (and fallback, if any) that served the request. usage Token and cost metrics per request. providers Returned by health endpoint; shows provider status.

# Chat with tools allowed by policy curl -s https://gateway.example.com/v1/chat \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATEWAY_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "route": "chat-primary", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize routing policy."}], "tools": [{"name": "fetch-user-profile"}] }' # Embeddings curl -s https://gateway.example.com/v1/embeddings \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATEWAY_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "route": "embed-primary", "input": ["context routing improves precision", "model gateway budgets control cost"] }'

{ "route_used": "chat-primary", "trace_id": "trace-abc123", "choices": [ { "message": { "role": "assistant", "content": "Context routing directs events based on metadata to reduce noise." } } ], "usage": { "prompt_tokens": 120, "completion_tokens": 64, "cost_usd": 0.0021 } }
Request size: 512 KB. Rate limits: default 100 requests per second per token. Tool schema size: 32 KB per tool definition.

400: malformed request or missing parameters. 401: invalid or expired token. 403: route blocked by policy. 429: rate limited; retry with backoff. 503: provider unavailable; check route_used and traces.

Configuration is declarative to keep changes reviewable and repeatable.

Define routes per model family (chat, completion, embedding). Set provider priority and fallback behavior. Include model-specific parameters such as max tokens and temperature. Sample route config: routes: - name: chat-primary family: chat providers: - name: provider-a model: gpt-4.1 temperature: 0.3 - name: provider-b model: claude-3 temperature: 0.3 fallback: true tools: allow: - fetch-user-profile - fetch-account-balance budgets: max_tokens: 4000 max_cost_usd: 0.10

Safety filters: PII scrubbing, allowed tools, blocked categories. Logging: redact sensitive fields before persistence. Tool access: align with the Context routing pattern if events trigger downstream actions. Policy checklist: Area Default Considerations PII scrubbing On Required for customer-facing apps. Tool allowlist Per route Keep tight to reduce blast radius. Blocked categories High risk blocked Align with trust and safety guidance. Logging redaction On Ensure trace logs exclude user identifiers.
Set soft and hard limits per service. Emit alerts to observability endpoints noted in the Runtime observability note.

Store configs in version control; changes land via pull requests. Include an ADR reference from the ADR template for significant policy shifts. Announce changes on the prose site at https://pruning-my-pothos.github.io/prose.

Apply configs in staging and run sample chat/completion/embedding calls. Confirm route_used and trace_id appear in responses and logs. Trigger a blocked category to verify safety filters respond with 403. Exceed soft budgets to confirm alerts fire.
Reapply the previous config version from version control. Disable a route by marking it inactive and redeploy. Remove tools from allowlists if misuse is detected.
Follow these steps to deploy the gateway. Review the platform overview first.
Kubernetes cluster or container runtime for the control plane. Access to provider credentials and allowed regions. TLS certificates for inbound traffic.

Deploy control plane helm repo add model-gateway https://example.com/charts helm upgrade --install mgw model-gateway/mgw --values values.yaml Seed routes and providers Apply routes/default.yaml and providers/openai.yaml to configure base models. Configure safety policies Enable PII scrubbing and tool allowlists via policies/safety.yaml. Smoke test Call the status endpoint and run a sample completion request.
Gateway control plane running with default routes. Safety policies applied. Connectivity to at least one provider verified.
Configure policies: Platform configuration Integration pattern: Resilient Workflows architecture Document changes with an ADR using the ADR template
The Model Gateway fronts multiple model providers behind a single contract. It handles routing, safety, and billing protections so teams can consume models without bespoke integrations.
Unified API for chat, completion, and embedding endpoints. Policy engine for safety, PII scrubbing, and allowed providers. Usage metering with budgets per service or project.
You need to swap model vendors without code changes. You want centralized safety and spending controls. You are building patterns like Resilient Workflows that depend on predictable responses.

Routes: map model families to providers and configurations. Policies: safety filters, allowed tools, and data handling rules. Budgets: soft and hard limits for cost control. Observability: traces and metrics emitted per call.

Route selection with fallbacks per model family. Safety filters: PII scrubbing, tool allowlists, and blocked categories. Budget enforcement: per-service cost and token limits. Observability hooks: trace IDs, route_used, and usage metrics on every response.
It does not replace platform-specific SDKs for advanced features. It does not store training data; keep prompts and outputs outside the gateway.

Use these steps to work with the gateway after installation. Code snippets are ready to copy and adjust.

curl Node Python curl -X POST https://gateway.example.com/v1/chat \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATEWAY_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"route":"chat-primary","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize routing policy."}]}' const res = await fetch('https://gateway.example.com/v1/chat', { method: 'POST', headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.GATEWAY_TOKEN}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json', }, body: JSON.stringify({ route: 'chat-primary', messages: [{role: 'user', content: 'Summarize routing policy.'}], }), }); const data = await res.json(); console.log(data.route_used, data.trace_id, data.choices?.[0]?.message?.content); import os import requests resp = requests.post( "https://gateway.example.com/v1/chat", headers={ "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['GATEWAY_TOKEN']}", "Content-Type": "application/json", }, json={ "route": "chat-primary", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize routing policy."}], }, timeout=15, ) resp.raise_for_status() data = resp.json() print(data["route_used"], data["trace_id"], data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]) Verification Confirm trace_id is present and route_used matches the intended route. Use the trace ID to find logs in observability dashboards.
Register tools with schemas; tools are allowed per policy. Align tool naming with the Context routing architecture when emitting events.
Expect trace_id in responses; use it to join logs described in the Runtime observability note. When fallbacks occur, the route_used field shows which provider responded.
Missing policies lead to rejected calls; confirm configuration. Overly broad tools increase risk; scope tools to routes. Forgetting budgets can cause noisy alerts; configure budgets early.

401 Unauthorized: rotate tokens and confirm the service principal is allowed on the route. 403 Forbidden: route or tool blocked by policy; check the policy store and budgets. 429 Too Many Requests: back off with jitter; raise limits only after verifying budgets. 503 Service Unavailable: check provider health and fallbacks; retry with circuit breakers.

Call succeeds with expected route_used and trace_id. Budget counters increment as expected for the service. Observability shows spans for the gateway call and downstream actions. Tools invoked match the allowlist; no unexpected tool calls appear in logs.

If a new route misbehaves, set it to inactive and revert to the prior route version in config. Disable problematic tools by removing them from the policy and redeploying. Lower budgets temporarily to contain cost while investigating.

sequenceDiagram participant App as App participant Gateway as Model Gateway participant Primary as Provider A participant Fallback as Provider B App->>Gateway: POST /v1/chat (route: chat-primary) Gateway->>Primary: Call with tools + policies alt Provider A healthy Primary-->>Gateway: Response + usage else Provider A down Gateway->>Fallback: Call fallback route Fallback-->>Gateway: Response + usage end Gateway-->>App: Response with route_used and trace_id
Review the API reference for endpoint details. If responses need more grounding, see Vector evaluation.

Welcome to Verse. This site is a technical documentation system, not a blog and not a personal wiki. It exists to demonstrate how technical knowledge can be structured, communicated, and maintained with clarity and intent. If you are new here, read this page first. It explains how the documentation is organized and how to use it effectively.

This documentation serves three purposes: To document platforms, interfaces, and systems in use or under study To demonstrate strong technical writing judgment To separate stable guidance from learning in progress Every section and page exists to serve a specific reader need. Pages are intentionally constrained to avoid confusion and cognitive overload.

This site follows the Diataxis documentation framework, which separates documentation into four distinct types. Each type answers a different question and requires a different writing style. The four documentation types are: Tutorials - learning by doing How-to guides - getting a task done Reference - precise, complete information Explanation - understanding concepts and decisions Pages are written to serve one purpose only. Mixing types is avoided on purpose. You do not need to know Diataxis to use this site, but it explains why the structure feels deliberate.

This section documents specific platforms, tools, and interfaces. You will find: Reference material such as APIs, configuration options, and commands How-to guides for installation, setup, and common usage tasks If you are asking “what does this do” or “how do I use this”, start here.

This section contains conceptual documentation. You will find: Explanations of system design choices Architecture overviews Decision guidance and trade-offs If you are asking “why is this designed this way” or “when should I use this approach”, this is the right place.

This section contains task-oriented guides. You will find: Clear goals Prerequisites Step-by-step instructions Expected outcomes These pages assume you already understand the basics. They are focused on getting something done, not on teaching concepts.

This section contains learning in progress. You will find: Experiments Observations Open questions Partial understanding Content here is intentionally exploratory and may change. These pages are not stable guidance and should not be treated as final documentation.

This section contains reusable documentation artifacts. You will find: Document skeletons Checklists Writing patterns Reusable structures Templates support the other sections. They are meant to be applied, adapted, and reused.

Use this site based on your intent: If you want to understand a system, read Systems and Design Patterns If you want to do something, go to How-To Guides If you need exact information, use Platforms and Interfaces If you want to see how thinking evolves, read Exploration Notes If a page feels calm and focused, that is intentional.
This site is not: A dumping ground for notes A chronological blog A marketing site A single-source tutorial It is a system designed to make technical knowledge usable.

This documentation is the technical foundation. Execution examples, case studies, communication artifacts, and creative writing live on the Prose site. Where relevant, documentation pages link outward to real-world applications and narrative context, for example https://pruning-my-pothos.github.io/prose.

documents.t: Good documentation is not about saying more. It is about saying the right thing, in the right place, for the right reason. That principle governs everything you see here.
Use this pattern when you need to combine LLMs, tools, and routing without losing control.
Multiple models and tools increase complexity and cost. Prompts and vibe coding drift without clear contracts. Safety and budgets are enforced inconsistently across entry points.

Gateway: routes requests, enforces budgets, and validates schemas (see Model Gateway). MCP contracts: predictable tool schemas and context delivery (see MCP overview). Routing rules: context-aware selection of tools/models (see Context Routing). Resilience: retries, fallbacks, compensations (see Resilient Workflows).

You need to swap models/providers without rewriting prompts and tools. You want vibe-coded prompts to stay within guardrails and budgets. You are exposing tools to multiple agents or apps with shared contracts.
Single-model, static prompt flows with no tool calls. Ultra-low-latency paths that cannot tolerate routing overhead.
Version prompts and tool schemas; lint prompts for required style cues. Enforce allowlists per route and per MCP tool. Log trace_id, route_used, and tool invocations for every call.
Docs: Prompt engineering & vibe coding Platform: Model Gateway usage Exploration: Prompt drift note
Use this pattern to ship AI capabilities with clear communication, enablement, and safeguards.
AI features land without clear guidance, leading to misuse and rework. Teams lack a repeatable way to communicate changes and expected adoption steps.
Pair every change with a concise comms plan, docs links, and a checklist for adoption and rollback.
Any change to prompts, routes, tools, or safety policies. New AI capabilities that require team-level adoption steps.

Use a single-page comms brief (see Change Communication Playbook). Link to authoritative docs (concepts, tasks, references) for the change. Provide enablement: office hours, sample commands, prompt packs. Capture decisions in ADRs; update sidebars and topics for discoverability.
Recipients can state what changed, why, and how to adopt. Docs are updated and linked; templates and prompts are available. Rollback steps are documented and tested.

Producers tag events with context fields: domain, entity, sensitivity, and operation. Routing rules evaluate context and map events to channels and consumers. Consumers receive filtered payloads and acknowledge delivery. Metrics feed into observability for latency, errors, and DLQ trends.

Rule engine: evaluates context and selects channels. Policy store: versioned rules stored with the service repo. Edge Messaging: enforces routing decisions at the edge. Observability stack: captures metrics and logs; see Runtime observability note.
Default deny: events without required metadata are rejected. Versioned rules: changes land via pull requests with ADR references. Test harness: simulate routing with sample events before deploy.
Platform: Edge Messaging configuration Trade-offs: Context routing trade-offs Guide: Publish a new platform guide
This pattern keeps messaging systems efficient by routing events using contextual filters and metadata.
Consumers drown in irrelevant events when producers broadcast widely. Ad hoc filters are inconsistent across teams.
Standardize routing rules based on event context: domain, entity, sensitivity, and consumer capability. Keep routing rules declarative and versioned.

Architecture: Context routing architecture When to use: When to use context routing Trade-offs: Context routing trade-offs Platform alignment: Edge Messaging overview Guide: Publish a new platform guide
Reduces consumer noise and processing costs. Improves compliance by minimizing data exposure. Encourages explicit ownership of routing rules.
Rule complexity can grow quickly if not curated. Additional metadata requirements on producers. Testing overhead to prevent regressions.
Keep a small set of required context fields. Reuse templates from the ADR template when changing routing rules. Run probes described in Vector evaluation to check retrieval and routing accuracy.
Platform: Edge Messaging API Guide: Publish a new platform guide Exploration: Runtime observability note

Use context routing when: Multiple services subscribe to the same event types but need different payload slices. You must enforce data minimization by default. You operate in environments with strict audit requirements. Avoid or simplify when: Only one consumer exists and volume is low. The platform already enforces strict schemas and narrow topics. Related: Architecture: Context routing architecture Platform: Edge Messaging usage Exploration: Runtime observability note

Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines a standardized way for models to consume tools and context with predictable schemas and controls. This overview explains when to adopt MCP, how it aligns with Verse patterns, and the guardrails required for safe use.

Ad hoc tool schemas increase integration cost and error rates. Models may invoke tools without sufficient guardrails, risking unintended side effects. Context delivery is inconsistent across platforms, leading to brittle prompts and reruns.

Define a shared contract for context, tools, and invocations so models can interact with systems predictably. Keep schemas versioned and discoverable, with capability negotiation between client and server.

You need multiple models or agents to consume the same toolset with minimal rework. You want platform-neutral contracts that work across providers or gateways. You plan to enforce safety, budget, and auditing consistently (see Model Gateway overview).
A single, tightly controlled runtime with static prompts and no tool calls may not benefit. If tools are highly bespoke and unlikely to be reused, MCP overhead might not be justified.

Client: sends requests, advertises capabilities (tooling, context formats), and receives results. Server: exposes tools, schemas, and context sources; enforces auth, rate limits, and safety. Gateway: optional front door that handles routing, budgets, and safety (see Model Gateway configuration). Observability: traces tool calls, context fetches, and errors; align with Runtime observability.

Client discovers server capabilities and supported MCP version. Client sends a request with tool name, arguments, and context references. Server validates auth, schema, and budgets; invokes the tool. Server returns result with metadata, usage, and trace IDs. Metrics and logs are emitted for auditing and tuning.

{ "version": "0.2.0", "capabilities": { "tools": [ { "name": "fetch_customer_profile", "schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "customer_id": {"type": "string"}, "fields": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}} }, "required": ["customer_id"] } } ], "context": [ { "name": "docs-index", "schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "query": {"type": "string"}, "top_k": {"type": "integer", "default": 5} }, "required": ["query"] } } ] } }

Auth: Use per-client credentials and short-lived tokens. Schema validation: Reject requests that do not match the published schema; return clear errors. Safety: Enforce tool allowlists per route; block high-risk actions unless explicitly permitted. Budgets: Apply per-client and per-tool rate limits; integrate with Model Gateway budgets for consistency. Observability: Require trace_id and route/tool metadata in logs and responses.

Use MCP tool contracts within the gateway to keep tool invocation predictable (Model Gateway usage). Combine with Context routing architecture to deliver only the context each tool needs. Apply Resilient workflows to handle timeouts, retries, and compensations around MCP tool calls.

Capability discovery works and returns the expected schema set. Requests with missing or invalid fields are rejected with clear errors. Tool calls include trace_id, route, and usage metadata for audit. Budgets and rate limits trigger alerts when exceeded.

Prototype MCP contracts in a staging server and capture notes in Exploration. Once stable, store schemas with the service repo and reference them from gateway configs. Record major contract changes in an ADR using the ADR template.

Orchestrator receives a task and defines a small plan. Calls the Model Gateway with guarded prompts and tool allowlists. Applies retries with jitter and circuit breakers per dependency. Runs compensating actions if a step fails after side effects. Emits traces and metrics for each attempt.

Orchestrator: coordinates steps and policies. Policy store: versioned prompts, tools, and budgets. Model Gateway: enforces routing, safety, and budgets. Observability: traces and metrics; see Runtime observability note.
Circuit breakers per dependency. Idempotency keys for side-effecting calls. Canary routes for new prompts or tools.

workflow: onboarding-summary routes: - name: chat-primary fallback: chat-secondary prompts: version: 3 lint: strict tools: - name: fetch-user-profile allow: chat-primary timeout_ms: 800 budgets: max_tokens: 2000 max_cost_usd: 0.05

Run replay tests with recorded inputs; assert deterministic fallbacks. Simulate provider failure to confirm compensations execute. Verify trace IDs appear in both Model Gateway logs and orchestrator spans.
Trade-offs: Resilient workflows trade-offs How-to: Publish a new platform guide Platform: Model Gateway usage
Resilient Workflows keep automation running even when model calls or services fail intermittently. They complement platform controls like the Model Gateway overview.
Model and service calls can degrade without notice. Downstream actions may be irreversible if not guarded.
Compose workflows with retries, compensations, and health-aware routing. Keep prompts, tools, and fallbacks versioned and observable.

When to use: When to use resilient workflows Architecture: Resilient workflows architecture Trade-offs: Resilient workflows trade-offs Platform alignment: Model Gateway usage Exploration: Runtime observability note
Reduces outage impact by isolating failures. Improves safety by gating actions behind policies and compensations. Enables gradual rollouts with canary routes and budgets.
Increased complexity in orchestration code. Additional latency from retries and fallbacks. More configuration to manage prompts, tools, and budgets.
Use templates from the ADR template for policy and architecture changes. Start with a small set of resilience controls, then expand. Reuse Model Gateway policies to avoid duplication.
Pattern: Resilient workflows architecture Platform: Model Gateway API Exploration: Runtime observability note

Use resilient workflows when: Model variability can affect correctness or safety. External dependencies fail intermittently. You need compensating actions for downstream calls. Avoid or simplify when: Manual approval already gates critical actions. Latency budgets cannot tolerate retries or fallbacks.
